purpose: The Perimeter — Kristy’s sourced answers for the parts of the store that have no barcode: produce, the butcher and fish counters, dairy, bulk bins, and the label terms used there. Entries are TOPICS, not flags: the perimeter answers questions, it does not score products. It is loaded separately from the ingredient KB and is NEVER fed into the verdict engine.

evidence_tiers.established: Strong scientific consensus, major health organization classification, or regulatory action in multiple countries. Settled enough to act on without debate.
evidence_tiers.credible_concern: Meaningful peer-reviewed evidence of harm exists. Debate is ongoing, but the signal is real and worth flagging, especially where a clean swap exists.
evidence_tiers.kristys_standard: The whole-food standard leads here even where regulators have not acted. Flagged as a standard, not as settled science. The difference is always stated.
evidence_tiers.time_tested: Foods with deep roots in human diets, eaten and trusted across generations, often long before modern studies existed. History is the evidence, and it is labeled that way. Absence of a clinical trial is not absence of value, and tradition is never dressed up as settled science.

no_answer: No solid answer on that one yet. Better said than guessed. The fish counter, the butcher, produce, dairy, the bulk aisle, and what a label term actually means are all covered.

entries.title: Salmon
entries.question: Is wild or farmed salmon better?
entries.decision: Wild salmon, frozen wild Alaskan before fresh farmed.
entries.why: Feed decides the fat, and a penned fish eats what it is given. Wild is the whole-food standard.
entries.short_answer: Two different animals sold under one name. Wild salmon eats krill and small fish across open ocean. Farmed salmon eats a ration of plant protein and vegetable oil, not krill.
entries.detail: That ration leaves farmed salmon with far more omega-6 and a much worse omega-3 to omega-6 ratio. Astaxanthin goes into the ration because the flesh comes out gray without it. Sea lice and the treatments used against them are the cost of penning fish that close together, and antibiotic use varies enormously by country of origin. The ratio is the claim, not the amount. Farmed salmon is fatter, so a serving can carry as much total omega-3 as wild or more; what the feed changes is the balance against omega-6, and that is the difference worth naming. Country of origin does most of the work on the rest: Norwegian farming runs close to zero antibiotic use on the back of vaccination, and other producing countries run far higher. The fish never swam anywhere, and it was colored to look like one that did.

entries.title: Beef
entries.question: Is grass-fed beef worth it?
entries.decision: 100% grass-fed or grass-finished beef.
entries.why: Grass after weaning, no grain and no feedlot. A grass finish gives you leaner beef with a different fat balance.
entries.short_answer: ‘Grass-fed’ alone can mean a grain finish. ‘100% grass-fed’ means grass after weaning, no grain. A farm selling direct can say how the herd ate to the end.
entries.detail: The federal grass-fed marketing standard was withdrawn in 2016, so a bare ‘grass-fed’ claim rests on the producer. The fat profile follows the finish, not the start, so grass to the end is the bar. Traditional food guides put meat from animals allowed to graze at the top, fat and organs included. A grazing farm sold direct, or a butcher who names the farm, is how to know the finish.

entries.title: Rotisserie chicken from the hot case
aliases: what is in a rotisserie chicken
is the deli rotisserie chicken injected
entries.question: Is the rotisserie chicken worth buying?
entries.decision: Pasture-raised rotisserie chicken, salt and spices only.
entries.why: A plain bird is chicken, salt and spices, roasted in the store. Phosphate and starch go in with a needle.
entries.short_answer: A rotisserie bird is a plain chicken or a solution bird. A plain one is chicken with salt and spices, roasted in the store. A solution bird was pumped with a seasoning solution before the spit. The sticker says which.
entries.detail: Two label rules do the work. 9 CFR 381.117(h): a raw poultry product with added solution must carry a descriptive designation stating the percentage of added solution as a number with the % sign, e.g. ‘contains 15% added solution of water and salt’, plus the common or usual name of every solution ingredient in descending order; the word ‘enhanced’ may not appear in the product name. 9 CFR 381.118(a): any poultry product fabricated from two or more ingredients lists them by common or usual name in descending order of predominance; ingredients at 2 percent or less may trail the list under a ‘contains 2% or less of’ line. 9 CFR 424.21 permits sodium and potassium phosphates in poultry ‘to decrease the amount of cooked out juices’, capped at 0.5 percent of total product, and sodium hydroxide only alongside phosphate at one part to four. FSIS’s labeling glossary defines a bone-in bird injected or marinated with broth, water, fat or flavor enhancers as ‘basted’ or ‘self basted’, about 3 percent solution, with the solution ingredients named on the label. At the shelf the two kinds read differently: a plain bird’s panel is one line (one store’s organic rotisserie chicken lists ‘organic chicken’ and nothing else); a solution bird lists water and its seasoning after the chicken, in descending order as 381.118 requires; a phosphate, a starch and a sweetener are the usual entries. On the sticker, the second word on the list settles it: ‘salt’ or ‘spices’ is a plain bird; ‘water’ followed by ‘sodium phosphate’, ‘modified food starch’, ‘sugar’ is a solution bird, roasted. Both are cooked chicken. One of them is also a marinade injection. Two federal label rules settle it; the ingredient list just needs reading.

entries.title: Ground beef
entries.question: What ground beef lean ratio should I get?
entries.decision: An organ blend, or 100% grass-fed ground beef.
entries.why: An organ blend folds liver and heart into a familiar grind.
entries.short_answer: Pick an organ blend, or ground beef with nothing added. How the cattle were raised is on the Beef card.
entries.detail: Both ‘ground beef’ and ‘hamburger’ cap at 30% fat, so the name is where the difference lives. ‘Ground chuck’, ‘round’ or ‘sirloin’ names the cut it came from. The ingredient list should be beef, with seasoning at most. ‘Ground beef’ may not contain added water, phosphates, binders or extenders, and may not have beef fat added as such. ‘Hamburger’ may. The ratio on the pack is lean to fat by weight. 80/20 is 20% fat; 90/10 is leaner. The name ‘ground beef’ allows no added water, phosphates, binders or extenders. 9 CFR 319.15(a) defines ‘Ground Beef’ as chopped fresh or frozen beef, fat capped at 30 percent, no added water, binders or extenders, with trimmed cheek meat the one allowed addition and capped at 25 percent. A product with liver or heart in it falls outside that definition, and 9 CFR 317.2 then requires a common or usual name or a truthful descriptive designation plus a full ingredient statement in descending order. ‘Ancestral blend’ and ‘primal blend’ are producer names for exactly this product, not standardized terms. Two label examples: one blend states 8 percent organ meats (4 percent liver, 4 percent heart, 92 percent muscle); another states 92 percent ground beef, 5 percent liver, 3 percent heart. Liver is the retinol-dense ingredient: the NIH fact sheet lists pan-fried beef liver at 6,582 mcg RAE per 3 ounces, against a tolerable upper intake of 3,000 mcg a day for adults. A blend that states its shares is plain ground beef with a measured amount of organ folded in. A blend carries its own descriptive name and a full ingredient list. By NIH figures, 3 ounces of pan-fried beef liver holds more than twice the adult daily vitamin A upper intake. Producers print shares such as 8 percent organ, or 5 percent liver plus 3 percent heart. Organs are part of eating the whole animal, and a blend puts them in a familiar grind.

entries.title: Eggs
aliases: Pasture-raised organic corn- and soy-free eggs
entries.question: What do cage-free, free-range, and pasture-raised eggs actually mean?
entries.decision: Soy-free, corn-free eggs from hens on pasture.
entries.why: A hen eats what she is given. Organic, pasture and feed words tell you about both her food and her life.
entries.short_answer: Look for pasture-raised, organic, and corn- and soy-free together. Next is soy-free organic pasture-raised, then organic pasture-raised. A certifier’s seal backs the pasture claim.
entries.detail: Both ‘soy-free’ and ‘corn-free’ have to be printed outright, because nothing else on the carton implies them, and most cartons never do. The claim clusters on small regional brands, farm stands and farmers markets rather than on the national pasture-raised labels, so the supermarket case is often the wrong place to look for it. Organic reaches the ration from a different direction: organic feed, no GMOs, no routine antibiotics, no added hormones. Pasture-raised paired with a third-party certification (Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved) is a real and audited claim about space, the strongest of the space words, and it still sits below feed here. Cage-free and free-range are weaker again, and the words on their own are not worth paying up for. Cage-free, free-range and pasture-raised describe how much room the hen had and whether she got outside, and not one of them says a word about what went in the trough. The standard is all three on one carton: what she ate, how it was grown, and how much room she had.

A feed claim says what is in the ration, not where it came from. Feed grown on the farm can be traced. Feed from several unnamed suppliers often cannot, and the carton does not say which.
“Vegetarian fed” means the hens were not fed animal byproducts; it does not describe outdoor access.
“Cage free” means no cages, not outdoor access. “Free range” adds outdoor access, which can be a small space.
‘Omega-3 enriched’ sets no amount. Two enriched cartons can differ a lot and both wear the same words.

Certified Humane is three different labels. Its pasture-raised tier sits well above its free-range tier. Its cage-free tier requires no outdoor access at all. The watchdog scores them 60, 50 and 30 on the same scale.
The labels the watchdog scores highest are Animal Welfare Approved, Biodynamic, Real Organic Project and Regenerative Organic Certified. A carton with no add-on label at all scores zero on that line.
Yolk color is not a feed tell. Deep orange comes from a varied diet or from marigold in the ration, and the carton never says which.
The yolk photo on the carton is artwork, not a sample.
A paler brown shell is not a fresher or older egg. Pigment goes on in the last hours before laying. A stressed hen, an older hen or a hurried lay leaves less of it.
A carton may legally hold the next size up, as long as the two sizes are not mixed. A ‘Large’ dozen can be Extra Large. It cannot be smaller.
The sell-by is not the pack date. Two cartons with the same sell-by can have been packed weeks apart. The three-digit code is the one that tells them apart.
Four to five weeks past the pack date, refrigerated, is the extension guidance. Count from the three-digit code, not from the sell-by.
Eggs age far faster on the counter than in the fridge. A carton left out at the store or at home has spent its window early.
A cold egg left out at room temperature can sweat. Moisture on the shell is where bacteria can take hold. Refrigerated eggs should not sit out more than two hours.
Keep the carton on a middle or lower shelf, not the door. The door swings warm every time it opens.
Store-bought eggs do not need washing before use. They were already washed and sanitized at the plant.

entries.title: Produce
entries.question: Is organic produce worth the extra money?
entries.decision: Grown without sprays first on skin-on produce, then organic.
entries.why: Surface residue leaves with a discarded peel. On berries and apples, you eat the skin along with the flesh.
entries.short_answer: A local grower’s “grown without sprays” on skin-on produce first, then organic. When organic runs thin, start with what gets eaten skin-on: berries, greens, apples, grapes, potatoes. Peeled fruit like avocado, kiwi, mango and citrus can wait.
entries.detail: The surface-residue reasoning is sound as a prioritization tool: the peel carries the residue, so what gets discarded carries it away. Organic is not the finish line: the standard still permits approved sprays when other controls fall short, so a local grower who grows without sprays sits above it. Avocado tests among the cleanest produce in the country. The part that was sprayed is the part that goes in the bin. Anything peeled goes in plain, however soft it looks. Avocado, kiwi, mango, banana, citrus and onion all test low. Soak the conventional eaten-whole ones. A baking soda soak takes more surface residue off than a rinse.

entries.title: Freezing what is about to turn
entries.question: How do I freeze produce before it goes off?
entries.decision: Briefly scalded vegetables for the freezer; fruit goes in raw.
entries.why: A brief scald stops the enzymes that would leave frozen beans gray and tasting of hay months later.
entries.short_answer: Freezing slows a vegetable down. It does not switch it off. The enzymes behind ripening and browning keep working in the freezer, slowly. Sixty seconds in boiling water switches them off.
entries.detail: Unblanched, a bag of beans comes out gray and tasting of hay months later, because the enzymes kept working. After the scald, the job is keeping air and ice crystals away from the food. Fruit is the exception and it is a real one: the enzymes that matter in fruit mostly affect appearance rather than flavor, and blanching would cook the texture out, so berries, banana and stone fruit go in raw. For vegetables the sequence is scald, chill hard in ice water to stop the cooking, dry, then freeze in a single layer before bagging. A tray first keeps the pieces separate instead of fusing into one brick you have to break with a knife. Air is the other enemy: what is called freezer burn is water subliming off the surface and leaving it dried and oxidised, and pressing the air out of the bag is most of the defense. Very high-water vegetables collapse whatever you do.
entries.kristy_take: Sixty seconds in boiling water, then straight into ice water. Dry the vegetables and freeze them on a tray before bagging, so the pieces stay separate.
sources: food-preservation guidance on enzyme inactivation and blanching times
work on sublimation and surface oxidation in frozen storage
buying_tips: A brief scald stops the enzymes that leave frozen beans gray and tasting of hay.
Sixty seconds in boiling water, then straight into ice water to stop the cooking.
Freeze it flat on a tray before bagging, or it fuses into one brick.
Press the air out of the bag. Air is what burns it.
Fruit needs no blanching. Berries, banana and stone fruit go in as they are.
Date the bag. Frozen is not indefinite.
watch_out: Freezing rescues nothing that has already started to turn. It holds what you put in.
High-water vegetables collapse on thawing: cucumber, lettuce, radish. Those are not freezer candidates.
pick_steps: Scald vegetables sixty seconds, then plunge them into ice water.
Dry them, freeze flat on a tray, then bag with the air pressed out.
Fruit goes in raw; date every bag.
entries.science: Enzymes keep working below freezing, so unblanched beans come out gray and tasting of hay. A brief scald ends them. Fruit skips it, since blanching would cook the texture out. Air dries and oxidizes the surface, which is freezer burn. Freezing holds what goes in and rescues nothing already turning. High-water vegetables like cucumber, lettuce and radish collapse on thawing.
entries.tier_note: That enzymes survive freezing and a brief scald denatures them is settled food preservation science, and almost every home freeze skips that step.

entries.title: Buying produce in season
entries.question: Does buying produce in season matter?
entries.decision: In-season produce from a small local grower, or frozen off-season.
entries.why: A January orange tastes better than a July one. Produce in season usually travels less and reaches you closer to ripe.
entries.short_answer: Yes. Supermarket produce is often harvested long before peak so it survives transit and storage. In season from a local farm or a garden is the top tier, organic or biodynamic. Out of season, organic frozen is the store fallback.
entries.detail: Supermarket produce is often harvested long before its peak nutritional value so it can survive transit and storage. Fresh from a garden or a local farm stand is best, organic or biodynamic and in season. Ask the grower how the crop was grown; a farm directory or farmers market lists local farms. Off-season, produce is shipped long distances or grown under conditions that trade flavor for availability, and organic frozen is the fallback. Broadly: tender greens and berries in spring, tomatoes and stone fruit in summer, squash and apples in autumn, citrus and hardy brassicas in winter. Season shows up in the size of the pile before it shows up anywhere else. Some produce ignores the calendar because it stores well (apples, onions, potatoes, winter squash, carrots) or because it was shipped from the other hemisphere, which is why ‘available’ and ‘in season’ are different words. Citrus peaks in the dead of winter, which is why a January orange tastes better than a July one.

entries.title: Butter
entries.question: Is grass-fed butter worth it?
entries.decision: Deep yellow 100% grass-fed butter: cream, and salt if salted.
entries.why: Carotene from the grass goes into the fat. The fatty-acid profile shifts with it, omega-3 included.
entries.short_answer: Cows on grass eat carotene, and it goes straight into the fat. So grass-fed butter runs deep yellow toward orange. Winter butter from the same dairy runs pale. The fat itself shifts modestly too.
entries.detail: Butter is cream, and salt if it is salted. A tub spread is a formulation, not butter: vegetable or seed oils, water, emulsifiers and flavoring, built to behave like butter. Within real butter, the grass difference is a feed difference showing up three ways at once: in the color, in the fat, and on the tongue. European-style butters are churned to a higher fat content, which is a separate axis from what the cows ate and the reason they bake and finish differently. The taste and the way it behaves in a hot pan are differences people can actually pick out, which is more than most sourcing claims manage. The fatty-acid profile shifts modestly too.

entries.question: Should you buy whole or low-fat milk?
entries.decision: Trusted raw milk from a farm, or low-temp pasteurized 100% grass-fed.
entries.why: Heat, homogenizing and skimming each change milk. Whole milk keeps its milkfat; reduced-fat milk has some removed.
entries.short_answer: Raw milk from a trusted local farmer comes first. Next is low-temp pasteurized, 100% grass-fed whole milk. Ultra-pasteurized milk is heated to about 280°F.

Whole milk is a whole-food-standard pick rather than a finding. A doctor’s advice for a specific person outranks a shelf standard.

entries.title: Rice and arsenic
entries.question: Should I buy white rice or brown?
entries.decision: White basmati from California, boiled in plenty of water.
entries.why: Arsenic concentrates in the bran, and the bran is what brown rice keeps.
entries.short_answer: Rice takes up more arsenic than other grains, and the bran holds most of it. Brown carries more than white; variety and origin matter more than color. White California basmati, rinsed and boiled in extra water, is the strong pick.
entries.detail: Rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains, and the bran holds most of it. Healthy Babies Bright Futures measured brown rice at 129 ppb against 86 for white. By variety, basmati averaged 55 ppb and sushi rice 57, while plain long-grain and parboiled both averaged 101. Origin moves it as much as color does. Rice grown in Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri and Texas tests highest, and California, India and Pakistan test lowest. Why the southern crop runs high is not settled. Those fields carry residue from decades of arsenical pesticides used on cotton, and the same fields also have sandier soil, which releases arsenic more readily than clay. Both explanations are published and neither has been shown to be the whole of it. Cooking is the other lever. Rinse the rice, boil it in a high ratio of water and pour the water off. The bran also carries phytic acid, so brown rice, when it is the choice, is bought organic and soaked overnight before cooking.

entries.detail: Steel-cut are the least processed, chewy and slow to cook. Rolled or old-fashioned are steamed and flattened. Instant are pre-cooked and often come pre-sweetened, and the flavored packets are mostly added sugar. The traditional step is the soak. Oats go into warm water overnight with a spoonful of yogurt, whey or apple cider vinegar, which reduces their phytic acid, and get cooked in the morning. Many traditional cooks toasted the oats in butter or ghee first for flavor. Conventional oats may be sprayed with glyphosate shortly before harvest to dry the crop, and organic farming does not allow glyphosate.

entries.title: Real honey vs. adulterated honey
entries.question: How do I know honey is real?
entries.decision: Raw unfiltered honey from a named local producer.
entries.why: Raw honey keeps its enzymes, and heating can compromise them. It is still a sweetener, just a real and old one.
entries.short_answer: Look for raw honey, ideally unfiltered, from a local producer you can name, with a label that reads only ‘honey’. Skip heated honey. Crystallized honey is normal. It is still a sugar, a sweetener to use with intention.
entries.detail: Raw honey has not been heated, so it keeps its enzymes, and unfiltered honey keeps more of what came from the hive. Heating does not spoil honey as a food, but the enzymes may be compromised. Commercial honey is often blended, and some has corn syrup added. A local producer you can name, and can ask whether the honey was heated or filtered, is the reliable route. Crystallizing is what raw honey does over time. Being an old, traditional food is a fair reason to prefer real honey. Tradition speaks to it being a real food, and it is still sugar.

entries.title: Dried vs. canned beans
entries.question: Are dried or canned beans better?

entries.title: “Natural”

entries.title: What “organic” covers — and what it doesn’t
entries.question: What does the organic seal actually guarantee?
entries.decision: Organic as the floor; the seal still allows approved sprays.
entries.why: It covers inputs and practices, not nutrition or processing. Approved sprays are still allowed.
entries.short_answer: Organic is a production standard. It excludes prohibited pesticides and GMOs. Animals get organic feed, with no routine antibiotics or added hormones. Approved sprays are allowed. An organic cookie is a cookie.
entries.detail: The National Organic Program defines organic as a set of permitted and prohibited INPUTS and practices, verified by certification. That is a real, enforced standard and worth something. What it is not is a nutrition claim: the seal is silent on whether the food is nutrient-dense or minimally processed, and ultra-processed foods can carry it in full compliance. Reading it as a shorthand for “good food” is the most common way it gets misused. Organic tells you how something was grown or raised, and you still have to look at what the thing actually is. Certified organic means no pesticides from the prohibited list. A short list of approved sprays is permitted, and it makes no claim at all about nutrient density, how well an animal was raised beyond the baseline, or how processed the food is. Organic is a floor, not the finish line: a grower who uses no sprays sits above it, and hydroponic crops can carry the seal too. Organic rules prohibit ionizing radiation. On non-organic foods, the Radura symbol and “treated with irradiation” identify this process.

entries.title: “Multigrain” vs. “whole grain”
entries.question: Is multigrain bread whole grain?
entries.decision: ‘100% whole grain’, a whole grain listed first.
entries.why: Multigrain allows every grain to be refined. Whole grain means the kernel is intact.
entries.short_answer: Not necessarily, and usually not. “Multigrain” only means more than one grain is in there. Every one of them can be refined. “Whole grain” means the kernel is intact, bran and germ included.
entries.detail: Neither term is a grading claim, but “whole grain” has a defined meaning tied to the intact kernel, while “multigrain” is a count. entries.title: “Lightly sweetened” and the sugar words
entries.question: Does “lightly sweetened” mean anything?
entries.decision: ‘Unsweetened’, or read the ‘Added Sugars’ line on the panel.
entries.why: ‘Lightly sweetened’ has no definition. The panel number is the one that cannot be spun.
entries.short_answer: No. It has no standardized definition. Neighboring terms do: “no sugar added” means none was added during processing. “Reduced sugar” means at least 25% less than a reference product. Only the added-sugar line on the panel cannot be spun.
entries.detail: This is a case where the regulated and the unregulated sit side by side on the same package. “Lightly sweetened” is not a defined claim. “No sugar added” and “reduced sugar” are defined, but neither means low: a juice with no added sugar is still concentrated fruit sugar, and 25% less than something very sweet is still sweet. Since added sugars became a separate line on the Nutrition Facts panel, the fastest honest read is to skip the front of the package entirely and look at that number, then check the ingredient list for the aliases: cane juice, syrups, concentrates. ‘Lightly sweetened’ is worth exactly what the marketing department decided it was worth. “No sugar added” leaves the food’s own sugars, and “reduced sugar” can still be a lot.

entries.title: “No artificial flavors” — what still gets in
entries.question: If it says no artificial flavors, what is the flavoring?
entries.decision: Short ingredient lists of recognisable foods over flavor claims.
entries.why: Natural flavors are still engineered. The legal difference is the starting material.
entries.short_answer: Natural flavors, still permitted and still made in a lab. The legal difference is the source material, not the processing. Natural flavors must start from a plant or animal. Either can be dozens of substances declared as two words.
entries.detail: The definition sits in 21 CFR 101.22: a natural flavor is derived from a spice, fruit, vegetable, edible yeast, herb, bark, bud, root, leaf, meat, seafood, egg or dairy product, whose significant function is flavoring. That is a rule about origin. It permits substantial processing, and it permits incidental additives (solvents, preservatives and carriers) to ride along inside the blend without separate declaration. So “no artificial flavors” is a true statement that answers a narrower question than most people think they are asking. The objection is the opacity rather than the word “artificial”: either way, two words on a panel stand in for a formulation nobody can see. A natural flavor has to start from something plant or animal derived; an artificial one does not. Both arrive as engineered compounds, and either can be a proprietary blend of dozens of substances declared as two words on the panel.

entries.title: Judging meat at the case
aliases: how to tell if meat is fresh
entries.question: How do I tell good meat from the case?
entries.decision: Sealed, leak-free meat with the newest ‘packaged on’ date.
entries.why: Oxygen turns a cut steak cherry-red; a vacuum-packed roast stays purple. Color alone cannot tell you freshness.
entries.short_answer: Color is the least useful signal, yet everybody uses it. Bright red beef has met oxygen; purple-red vacuum-packed beef has not. Both are fine. Better checks: a sealed package with no leaks, no off smell or slime.
entries.detail: Beef pigment turns bright red within minutes of oxygen exposure and oxidizes browner over days. That is surface chemistry, not spoilage, which is why a vacuum-sealed roast looks purple and a freshly cut steak looks cherry-red. The liquid in a tray is called purge; the check is the package itself, fully sealed, with no holes, tears or punctures, and not leaking meat juices. Sell-by dates are set by the store. Trust your nose over any of them. Dull brown at the edges means it has been cut a while.

entries.title: Chicken
entries.question: Which cut of chicken should I buy?
entries.decision: Air-chilled pasture-raised whole chicken, then bone-in, skin-on thighs.
entries.why: Thighs carry more fat and flavor, so they stay juicy and are hard to overcook. The skin renders and bastes as they cook.
entries.short_answer: Whole bird: lowest cost per pound, and the carcass makes stock. Thighs carry more fat and flavor, and are hard to overcook. Breast is lean and dries fast. Bone-in, skin-on cuts cost less and cook better than boneless skinless.
entries.detail: Dark meat comes from muscles the bird actually used, so it carries more fat and stays juicy across a wide window of doneness. Breast is a low-use muscle: lean, quick, unforgiving. Bones conduct heat slowly and skin renders and bastes, which is why bone-in skin-on thighs are the most forgiving thing in the case. Boneless skinless breast is convenience paid for twice, once at the register and again in how fast it dries. A whole bird broken down at home gives you both kinds of meat plus a frame for broth, at the lowest cost per pound in the store. Thighs are dark meat: more fat, more flavor, and very hard to overcook. Breast is lean and fast and goes dry the moment you look away. Bone-in and skin-on cost less and cook better than boneless skinless, which is the most expensive way to buy the same bird. A whole bird yields both meats and a stock frame; water-chilled packs can hold retained water.

entries.title: Mercury by fish
aliases: which fish are low in mercury
entries.question: Which fish are low in mercury and which are high?
entries.decision: Sardines, anchovies, salmon and canned light tuna, small and short-lived.
entries.why: Mercury tracks size and lifespan. The big long-lived predators carry the most.
entries.short_answer: It tracks size and lifespan almost perfectly. Small, short-lived fish carry the least. Big long-lived predators carry the most. Sardines, salmon and canned light tuna sit at the bottom. Swordfish, shark, king mackerel and bigeye tuna sit at the top.
entries.detail: Methylmercury accumulates up the food chain, so a fish that ate thousands of smaller fish across twenty years carries far more than one that lived two years on plankton. Ocean fish also carry selenium, which counteracts mercury, and studies that count mercury alone leave it out. Small wild fish such as sardines, anchovies, herring and mackerel give the most for the least. Anything about a personal medical situation belongs with a doctor. Canned light tuna is usually skipjack.

entries.title: Which farmed fish are worth buying
entries.question: Is farmed fish worth buying?
entries.decision: Wild fish first; shellfish is the one exception.
entries.why: ‘Farmed’ is not a verdict. Mussels and oysters feed themselves by filtering water.
entries.short_answer: It depends entirely on the species and the operation, never on the word ‘farmed’. Farmed mussels, oysters and clams are the standout: they filter water and need no feed. Farmed trout, arctic char and barramundi are generally well regarded.
entries.detail: Aquaculture is not one thing. A rope of mussels hanging in a bay feeds itself by filtering water and needs no feed at all. Farmed fish are another matter: crowded pens, a ration of plant protein and vegetable oil, and in some farms routine antibiotics and added color. Traditional food guides put farmed salmon, catfish and trout on the avoid list. So farmed shellfish is the farmed pick, and wild is the pick for fish.

entries.title: Seafood seals: MSC, ASC, BAP
entries.question: Do the sustainability seals on seafood mean anything?
entries.decision: Wild fish with a named origin and catch method.
entries.why: Each seal answers one narrow question about stock or farm practice. None speaks to freshness or the fish as food.
entries.short_answer: The blue MSC label covers wild fishery management; ASC and BAP audit farms. None is a health claim. Wild, a named origin and a catch method say more.

entries.question: How do I tell if this particular fruit or vegetable is any good?
entries.decision: The heavier of two same-size pieces, for more juice.
entries.why: Compare two pieces in your hands. More weight means more water rather than pith, a better guide than color.
entries.short_answer: Each item has one or two checks that work, almost never color. Heavy for its size is the near-universal one. Smell the stem end on anything that ripens off the plant. Turn berry containers over, where mold starts.
entries.detail: Fruit that keeps ripening after picking (melon, peach, avocado, banana, mango, pear) gives you smell and give as signals. Fruit that does not ripen further once picked (berries, citrus, grapes, pineapple, cherries) has to be bought ready, so those checks are about weight and damage instead. Vegetables are mostly a firmness question: a limp stalk or a rubbery skin means it has been out of the ground a while and lost water. The single best habit is picking up two of the same thing and comparing them by weight. The heavier one is almost always better.

entries.title: Berries
entries.question: How do I pick a good carton of berries?
entries.decision: Berries from a local farm, grown without sprays, then organic.
entries.why: The bottom berries carry the weight and mold first, while the top can still look fresh.
entries.short_answer: Turn the container over first. The bottom fruit carries the load, so it bruises and molds first. A dry, clean underside means it was packed recently and has not sat wet. Juice or a fuzzy spot means decay is running.
entries.detail: Berries do not ripen after picking. Unlike a peach or a cantaloupe, what is in the carton is exactly what you are buying. There is no counter-ripening to rescue an underripe punnet, and no reason to buy firm and wait. That makes the carton itself the whole decision. Weight and moisture are what work against it: the bottom layer carries the load, condensation inside a clamshell keeps that layer damp, and mold spreads berry to berry by contact. Clamshells also get re-stacked at the store, so a fresh-looking top layer can sit on fruit that arrived days earlier. Buy them cold, keep them dry, and wash them at the moment you eat them rather than when you unpack. The top layer stays presentable long after the carton has turned, and one furry berry takes the punnet.

entries.title: Making produce last the week
entries.question: How do I keep produce from going off before I use it?
entries.decision: Unwashed produce for storing; wash it when you use it.
entries.why: Water left on a leaf or berry is where mold starts. Keeping greens dry gives them longer in the drawer.
entries.short_answer: Three rules cover most of it. Keep ripening-gas fruit away from greens and berries. Do not wash anything until you use it. Keep a short list out of the fridge: tomatoes, potatoes, onions, garlic, whole melon, unripe stone fruit.
entries.detail: Apples, bananas, avocados, tomatoes and stone fruit give off the ripening gas, and greens, broccoli, cucumbers and berries are ethylene sensitive and wilt fast beside it. Ethylene is a plant hormone that triggers ripening and it works on neighbors, which is why a bowl of apples ages the lettuce next to it. Moisture is the other half: water sitting on a leaf or a berry is where mold starts, so the rinse belongs at the moment of eating rather than at unpacking. Cold wrecks texture and flavor in a few specific things. Tomatoes go mealy below about 55F, potatoes convert starch to sugar and brown oddly when cooked, and onions and garlic soften and sprout. Herbs and asparagus keep best standing in a little water like cut flowers, and greens keep best dry with a towel in the bag.

entries.title: Reviving wilted greens
entries.question: Can I bring limp greens back, or are they finished?
entries.decision: Limp greens without decay, ready for a cold-water soak.
entries.why: Cold water refills a limp leaf’s slack cells. As the water returns, the leaf stands firm again.
entries.short_answer: Most limp greens are thirsty, not spoiled. Water pressure in the cells holds a leaf rigid. When it drops, the leaf goes limp, but intact cells take the water back. Thirty minutes in cold water restores most of it.
entries.detail: The same mechanism explains why the trick is worth doing on more than lettuce. Celery, carrots, radishes, chard, kale and soft herbs all go limp by the same route and all firm up again. Cutting a sliver off the stem end first matters for anything with a stem, because the vessels seal and a fresh cut lets water move again, exactly as it does for cut flowers. Cold matters too. Cold water is taken up more readily and it firms the cell walls at the same time. Bagged, pre-washed greens revive least, because they have already been cut and a cut edge does not reseal. What does not come back is anything that has actually started to break down.
entries.kristy_take: Give wilted greens half an hour in cold water, then dry them before putting them away. Yellowing, slime or a smell means decay; a soak cannot bring those leaves back.

entries.title: Cream, half-and-half, and ‘creamer’
entries.question: What is the difference between cream and coffee creamer?
entries.decision: 100% grass-fed cream from a small dairy, not ultra-pasteurized.
entries.why: Cream has a legal fat minimum. Creamer is oil, sweetener and emulsifiers built to imitate it.
entries.short_answer: Cream is dairy with a legal fat minimum. ‘Non-dairy creamer’ is not dairy at all. It is typically water or corn syrup solids, an oil, and emulsifiers, flavors and thickeners built to imitate cream. Compare the two lists.
entries.detail: Heavy cream is at least 36% milkfat, light whipping 30 to 36, half-and-half 10.5 to 18. Standards of identity fix what cream can mean, which is why those fat percentages are consistent across every carton. Creamer has no such standard because it is a formulated product. The oil in it is usually a refined seed oil, not milkfat, and the sweetness usually comes from corn syrup solids or sugar, with the flavored versions adding more of both. Some cartons of real cream carry stabilizers like carrageenan or gellan gum, so a short list is worth checking on the dairy side too. Whole milk, half-and-half or real cream all do the job with a list you can read out loud. Read the two ingredient lists side by side and it takes three seconds. rBST is a synthetic hormone given to cows for milk production. The certified organic rules bar this growth hormone. Start with certified organic cream or half-and-half. Follow with a carton stating the cows were not treated with rBST, then one with neither. US companies need not label rBST use.

entries.title: Flour: bleached, enriched, whole
entries.question: Which flour should you buy, and what does ‘enriched’ mean?
entries.decision: Organic sprouted flour, or fresh-ground whole grain, soaked.
entries.why: Whole grain flour keeps the bran and germ, and soaking or sprouting is how those were traditionally made digestible.
entries.short_answer: Freshly ground organic whole grain flour, soaked before baking, is the top rung. Organic sprouted flour is next, with the soaking step done. Unbleached white is a limited use. Skip bleached white flour, and whole grain flour used without soaking.
entries.detail: Refining strips the bran and germ and leaves the starchy endosperm, which is what makes white flour pale and shelf-stable. Whole grain flour keeps them, along with the phytic acid in the bran. Soaking the flour overnight with a little acid, or buying flour made from sprouted grain, is the traditional answer. The germ also carries oil, and milled flour stored for long periods, particularly in open bins, turns rancid. Fresh-ground from a small mill, bought in small amounts and kept cold, is the way around that. On white flour, the label must bear the word “Bleached” when a bleaching ingredient was used. Bromated flour has potassium bromate added. Enriched means B vitamins and iron were added back after refining took them out.

entries.title: Whole spices and toasting
entries.question: Are whole spices worth the trouble over ground?
entries.decision: Organic whole spices, bought small, ground as you go.
entries.why: The aroma is volatile oil. Grinding opens the surface up and it leaves from there.
entries.short_answer: A spice’s flavor is its oil, and that oil escapes into the air. Whole, it stays sealed inside the seed or bark for a couple of years. Ground, it is gone within months. Grind as you go.
entries.detail: Toasting is worth separating from grinding. A dry pan over medium heat until the smell arrives across the kitchen does two things: it drives volatile compounds to the surface and it starts browning reactions in the seed that build flavors that were not there before. Toast whole, then grind, and use it; toasted spice fades faster than raw whole spice, so it is not something to do in a batch and store. A blade grinder is adequate and a mortar is better for anything you want texture from. A handful of spices are only sold ground because the whole form is impractical to break down at home, and those are worth buying in the smallest quantity you will actually finish. What you are buying in a spice is volatile oil. Ground, the surface area jumps and the same oil is off into the air within months, which is why a jar of ground cumin that smells of nothing is not spoiled, it is just empty. Warming them first drives the oils out where you can taste them.
entries.kristy_take: Whole, and grind what you need. A jar of ground spice is a jar with a clock on it.

entries.title: Telling when fats have turned
aliases: how to tell if oil is rancid
entries.question: How do I tell if nuts, oil or flour have gone rancid?
entries.decision: Oil in a dark bottle, finished within two months.
entries.why: Oxidized oil has a smell nothing else has. No date on the package will tell you.
entries.short_answer: Nuts, whole-grain flour and oils all carry fat that goes off. The tell is a smell like old paint, crayons, putty, or a dusty cupboard. The printed date does not predict it. Heat, light and air set the clock.
entries.detail: Oxidation is fat reacting with air, and light, heat and time all speed it up. That is the whole reason good olive oil comes in dark glass and gets stored away from the stove, and why whole-grain flour keeps months while white flour keeps almost indefinitely. The peppery catch at the back of the throat in fresh olive oil is a different sensation from the flat bitter scratch of a rancid one, and the difference is learnable in a single side-by-side taste. Once you can smell it, the bulk bin, the back of the pantry and the half-used oil bottle all become easy calls. The tell is a smell most people already know without a name for it. Nothing on the label predicts it, because the clock starts at pressing or milling and runs on heat, light and air rather than on the printed date.
sources: UC Davis Olive Center sensory standards for olive oil defects

America’s Test Kitchen “How to Tell If Olive Oil Is Rancid” https://www.americastestkitchen.com/articles/1224-how-to-tell-if-olive-oil-is-rancid (heat, air, light, and time will wreck the best olive oil; rancid oil has a distinctive smell like varnish, putty, old walnuts, or crayons, and rancidity is more obvious in the mouth, so take a tiny sip when in doubt; store cool, dark, tightly capped, and use it up promptly)

entries.title: Buying real extra-virgin olive oil
entries.question: How do I buy real extra-virgin olive oil, and what do the grades mean?
entries.decision: Extra virgin olive oil with a recent harvest date.
entries.why: Olive oil is widely adulterated. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ all mean refined oil.
entries.short_answer: Extra virgin uses no heat or solvent, and has to pass lab and taste tests. ‘Pure’, ‘classic’ and ‘light’ are refined oil with some virgin added. Look for a recent harvest date, a dark bottle and one country of origin.
entries.detail: Grade and provenance are two separate checks and a bottle has to pass both. On grade: pomace oil is solvent-extracted from the paste left after pressing and is a different product; ‘first cold pressed’ is a legacy phrase with no added legal force. On provenance: ‘packed in [country]’ names where it was bottled, not where the olives grew, and ‘product of’ is the phrase that names the origin. A harvest date beats a best-by date every time, because the oil degrades from the day it is pressed. Dark glass or tin protects it from light, and a price that is unusually low for extra-virgin is a flag rather than a find. Extra virgin is mechanically extracted with no heat or solvent and has to pass both a chemical limit and a taste panel. Virgin is the same process with a looser limit. ‘Light’ refers to color and taste rather than calories. Past the grade, olive oil is one of the more adulterated products in the store.

entries.title: Grains beyond rice
entries.question: What else should I be buying besides rice?
entries.decision: Organic whole grains, soaked overnight before cooking.

entries.detail: Hulled barley is minimally processed to remove only the tough inedible outer hull. Pearl barley has been polished to remove some or all of the outer bran layer along with the hull. Store-bought bulgur is parboiled and dried rather than soaked or sprouted, and quick-cooking grains skip the soak too. Variety is worth it on its own terms, since rotating grains means no single crop is the base of every meal. Buckwheat is not wheat at all. Millet and sorghum carry no gluten. entries.title: Buying bottled water
entries.question: Which bottled water should I buy?
entries.decision: Spring water from a named spring, in glass.
entries.why: Spring water comes from a place. Purified is a process run on whatever came out of the tap.
entries.short_answer: Two products share one shelf. Spring water is defined by its underground source. Purified water is defined by its treatment, often of city water. Its label need not name the source.
entries.detail: The type on the label is a federal standard of identity, so it is the one word on the bottle that has to be earned. Spring, artesian and mineral name a source. Purified, distilled, deionized and reverse osmosis name a process. Mineral water is spring water carrying at least 250 parts per million of total dissolved solids picked up from the ground, and no minerals may be added to it, which is why the term still means something. Do not shop this on mineral content. Reverse osmosis removes dissolved solids by design, so a purified bottle reads lower on paper and that is the equipment working exactly as intended, not evidence against it. Provenance is the argument, and it is the only one that holds. Spring water is defined by where it came from: an underground formation that flows to the surface on its own, collected there or from a bore hole in the same formation, and carrying the composition that water had before treatment. Purified water is defined by what was done to it, which is distillation, deionization or reverse osmosis, run on whatever the feed water happened to be. That feed water is frequently a municipal system, and here the labeling rule does the arguing: a bottler drawing from a community water system has to say so on the label, unless the water was purified, which lifts the requirement. Pass on water with natural flavors or artificial flavoring; those terms do not name the individual flavoring ingredients.
sources: 21 CFR 165.110 — FDA standards of identity for bottled water: spring, artesian, mineral, purified, and the community-water-system labeling requirement

entries.title: Front vs. back
aliases: how to read a food label
entries.question: Where on a package should I actually be looking?
entries.decision: A short list of recognizable foods, read on the back.
entries.why: The front is written by marketing. The back is written by law.
entries.short_answer: The front is advertising. The back is regulated. Front words like natural, wholesome and farm fresh come from marketing, and only some are legally defined. The ingredient list and Nutrition Facts panel have to be true. Turn it over first.
entries.detail: This is the one habit that makes every other label question easy. Nearly all of the confusion in a grocery store comes from front-of-pack language, which is written to imply more than it commits to, and almost none of it comes from the panel on the back, which is defined down to the font. Three things on the back do most of the work: the ingredient list in descending order by weight, the added-sugars line, and the serving size the numbers are based on. When the front and the back disagree, the back is the one that had to be checked. Every phrase on the front (natural, wholesome, farm fresh, made with real, lightly sweetened) is chosen by a marketing team, and only some of them have any legal definition at all. The ingredient list and the Nutrition Facts panel have to be true and have to follow a format. Turn it over first, and the front becomes noise.

entries.title: Ingredients are in weight order
entries.question: How do I read an ingredient list properly?
entries.decision: Ingredients led by foods, ahead of split sugars or flour.
entries.why: The list runs in weight order. Split sugars keep any one of them from climbing it.
entries.short_answer: Ingredients run heaviest first, so the first three are most of the package. Everything after ‘contains 2% or less of’ is a trace, in any order. Watch for split sugars, each listed separately so none climbs the list.
entries.detail: The weight-order rule is the most useful thing on any package, because it turns a list into a ranking. A bread whose first ingredient is ‘whole wheat flour’ is a different food from one whose first ingredient is ‘enriched wheat flour’, whatever the bag says. The 2%-or-less clause exists because ordering trace additives serves nobody, and it also means everything below that line is a rounding error. Sugar splitting is legal and common, and the added-sugars line on the Nutrition Facts panel is the counter to it, because it totals them all whatever they were called. A product can list cane syrup, dextrose, juice concentrate and honey separately so no single one climbs the list, when together they would sit near the top.

entries.title: Judging any seal on any package
entries.question: How do I know if a seal on a package means anything?
entries.decision: A seal naming a program with an outside auditor.
entries.why: A badge a company gave itself has neither. Each real seal covers one scope.
entries.short_answer: Ask three questions of any seal. Who set the standard? Is it published? Does an independent body audit against it? A company’s own badge answers none of them. No seal covers what it never set out to measure.
entries.detail: The gap between a certification and a marketing badge is entirely in the audit. Real programs publish their standard, so anyone can read exactly what was checked, and they send inspectors. The second half of reading a seal is scope: an organic seal covers inputs and practices and says nothing about welfare beyond a baseline, a welfare seal says nothing about pesticides, and a non-GMO seal addresses one issue only. Stacking seals on a package does not make it a better food, it makes it a food that paid for several audits. The ingredient panel still decides what the thing actually is. A badge a company created for its own products answers none of the three questions. USDA Organic, Real Organic Project, Certified Humane, Animal Welfare Approved, Global Animal Partnership and the Non-GMO Project all publish standards and use outside auditors. Real Organic Project sits on top of the organic seal and requires soil-grown crops and pastured animals. A farm that sells direct, where the grower answers questions about sprays, feed and pasture, reaches past what any seal audits. What no seal tells you is anything it never set out to measure.

entries.title: ‘Cold-pressed’, ‘expeller-pressed’, ‘refined’
entries.question: What do ‘cold-pressed’ and ‘expeller-pressed’ mean on an oil?
entries.decision: Cold-pressed or expeller-pressed olive or coconut oil.
entries.why: Expeller and cold-pressed are both mechanical. Most supermarket oil is neither.
entries.short_answer: Expeller-pressed means a mechanical screw press with no solvent, though friction still generates heat. Cold-pressed is the same press with the temperature held down. Most supermarket cooking oil is neither. It is solvent-extracted, then refined, bleached and deodorized.
entries.detail: Extraction and refining are two separate steps and both matter. Mechanical pressing leaves more of the original flavor, color and aroma in the oil, which is exactly why unrefined oils taste like the thing they came from and refined ones taste like nothing. Solvent extraction pulls far more oil out of the same seed, which is why it dominates at commercial scale. In the US ‘cold-pressed’ has no federal definition for most oils, so it carries less weight on a sunflower bottle than on an olive one. But the press only sorts oils that already clear the bar. Which oil it is settles the purchase first, and the pressing decides between two good ones after that. Two of these words describe pressing and one describes what happens afterwards. For olive oil in the EU, cold-pressed is a defined temperature limit. “Pure” and “refined” both describe oil stripped of color, flavor and aroma.

entries.title: ‘Sugar-free’ and what replaced the sugar
entries.question: If it says sugar-free, what is doing the sweetening?
entries.decision: ‘Unsweetened’; on ‘sugar-free’, read which substitute is listed.
entries.why: ‘Sugar-free’ is a defined claim about what came out. The list names what went in.
entries.short_answer: Something else, named on the ingredient list. ‘Sugar-free’ is defined as under half a gram of sugar per serving. The sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol or a high-intensity sweetener. ‘Unsweetened’ generally means nothing sweet was added at all.
entries.detail: ‘Sugar-free’ answers a Nutrition Facts question and says nothing about what took sugar’s place, which is why the ingredient list matters more here than on almost any other claim. Sugar alcohols appear by name and are also totalled on the panel; high-intensity sweeteners appear in the list and are used in tiny amounts. ‘Unsweetened’ has no formal FDA definition and in practice means no sweetener of any kind, including the non-caloric ones, which makes it the cleaner word to look for on yogurt, plant milk and apple sauce. ‘Naturally sweetened’ has no definition at all and covers honey, maple syrup and juice concentrate. Under ‘sugar-free’, the sweetness comes from a sugar alcohol (erythritol, maltitol, xylitol) or a high-intensity sweetener (stevia, monk fruit, sucralose, aspartame). ‘Unsweetened’ is the plainer word, and the two are not interchangeable.

entries.title: Seafood labels: wild, farm-raised, origin
entries.question: What has to be on a seafood label?
entries.decision: Wild-caught whole or skin-on fish, species, method and country named.
entries.why: All three are required on unprocessed seafood. Origin can mean where it was processed.
entries.short_answer: Most unprocessed fish and shellfish at retail must show the species, wild-caught or farm-raised, and the country of origin. Federal country-of-origin labeling requires it. The catch: origin can mean where it was processed, not where it was caught.
entries.detail: Country-of-origin labeling covers unprocessed fish and shellfish and is genuinely useful, since it turns ‘farm-raised, product of ___‘ into a readable pair rather than a guess. Two limits are worth knowing. Cooked, breaded or otherwise processed seafood falls outside the rule. And species naming has a long history of substitution, where one fish is sold under another species name, which is a far bigger problem on a bare fillet than on a whole fish or a piece with the skin left on. Buying whole, buying skin-on, and buying from a counter that can answer the origin question are the practical defenses. Country-of-origin labeling is one of the few places a store must tell you where food came from.

entries.title: Serving size and the numbers under it
entries.question: Why do the numbers on the panel look so low?
entries.decision: Packs compared at matching serving sizes, times servings per container.
entries.why: Every number is per serving. Half of what looks reasonable is a third of the package.
entries.short_answer: Because every number on the Nutrition Facts panel is per serving. The servings-per-container line says how many the package holds. ‘About 2.5 servings’ means multiplying everything by two and a half. Serving sizes reflect what people typically eat.
entries.detail: This is the easiest number on a package to misread, and it is not an accident that it sits at the top in small type. The reference amounts are fixed by the FDA per food category, so competing products in the same category are genuinely comparable, which is the useful thing about them. What they are not is a recommendation. The 2016 label rules made serving sizes more realistic, put added sugars on their own line, and required dual-column labelling on packages that could plausibly be finished in one sitting. Read from the top down: servings per container first, serving size second, then the numbers. Serving sizes are set by regulation to reflect what people typically eat, not what is good for anyone, and larger single-serve packages now have to show a per-package column too.

entries.title: “Artificial color” and what it need not name
entries.question: What does “artificial color” mean on an ingredient list?
entries.decision: Colors named from food; skip ‘artificial color’ and ‘color added’.
entries.why: Certified dyes must be named. The rest, titanium dioxide among them, may hide under a group term.
entries.short_answer: Two rules, split on certification. A certified dye must be declared by name, so “Red 40” always appears as itself. A color exempt from certification may ride as “Artificial Color” or “Color Added.” Titanium dioxide is one of those.
entries.detail:
The split is written into 21 CFR 101.22(k). Paragraph (k)(1) covers color additives subject to certification and requires each to be declared by the name in its own regulation, dropping the “FD&C” prefix but keeping “Lake” where it applies. Paragraph (k)(2) covers color additives not subject to certification and permits the collective terms instead, offering “Colored with ______” as the alternative that names the substance. Titanium dioxide is listed at 21 CFR 73.575, which sets the one percent ceiling and states that batches are exempt from certification.

So the generic phrase is a signal rather than a blank. Where a panel reads “artificial color” with no number beside it, the color is one federal rules did not require to be named, and the panel alone cannot say which.

A certified dye must be declared by its own name, so “Red 40” and “Blue 1” always appear as themselves. A color exempt from certification does not have to: federal labeling rules let it ride as “Artificial Color,” “Artificial Color Added” or “Color Added.” Titanium dioxide is the white pigment used for opacity in candy shells, frosting, chewing gum and creamy dressings, capped at one percent of the food by weight. A label may name it outright as “colored with titanium dioxide,” and nothing requires that. The EU removed it from food after a review by its food safety authority, and food makers there took it out. US rules still allow it. The plain move at the shelf is to skip a list carrying a generic color term and take one with no added color, or a color named from a food.

entries.card_why: Kefir is what a dairy does with milk it wants to keep, and it has been doing it for centuries. The grains turn it tangy and thick and it holds for weeks where the milk holds for days. The rule is the milk’s rule: the farm is the product. Buy it from the herd you would drink from raw, as close to the culture date as the case allows.
entries.short_answer: Raw kefir is a live ferment and it has to be sold cold. Anything shelf-stable was heat-treated after culturing, which ends the thing you were buying it for.
entries.detail: Kefir carries a wider mix of cultures than yogurt and pours rather than spoons. Made from raw milk it is the same sourcing question as the milk: a named farm, a small herd, a cold chain. Plain is the only version worth buying. The flavored tubs carry the added sugar of a dessert and the ferment becomes the excuse.
entries.kristy_take: Same farm as the milk, or it is just a drink.
buying_tips: Kefir is only as good as its milk, and the ferment stays live only when cold.

entries.title: Raw aged cheese
entries.question: Is raw milk cheese worth buying?
entries.decision: Aged raw milk or lait cru cheese, 60 days minimum.
entries.why: Aged raw-milk cheese tastes of one herd and season, and its maker has to know the milk.
entries.card_why: Aged raw-milk cheese is the raw dairy nobody has to hunt for. US rules allow it at sixty days and up, so a decent cheese counter already keeps a case of it. Sixty days of aging is a technology of its own. It is the reason an aged raw cheddar tastes of the place it came from. A young commodity block tastes of very little. The organizing principle is the milk’s: ask who made it, from which herd, and how long it sat.
entries.short_answer: It is the raw dairy nobody has to go looking for. US law lets raw-milk cheese aged sixty days or more sell across state lines. It sits in ordinary cheese cases. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way.
entries.detail: The sixty-day rule is why raw cheese is legal at US retail where raw milk often is not. Aging concentrates the cheese and develops it, and a raw-milk cheese carries the character of one herd and one season in a way a standardized pasteurized curd is designed not to. A staffed counter can usually name the maker, the animal and the age, which is exactly the information the rind label is too small to hold. Raw-milk cheese sits in the case beside everything else: no farm visit, no herdshare, no state-by-state map. Most traditional European cheeses are made this way, which is why so many qualify.

entries.title: Sprouts
entries.question: Are sprouts worth buying?
entries.decision: Organic broccoli, radish or mung sprouts; skip alfalfa and soy.
entries.why: Weston A. Price guidance accepts sprouted seeds but not alfalfa or soy, and eats sprouts lightly steamed, not raw.
entries.card_why: Sprouts are about as alive as produce gets, a seed caught mid-decision, sold days old. That is the appeal, and it is also the whole handling question. The warm damp days that sprout a seed are the same days that sprout everything else. A grower who keeps them cold from the sprouting room to the case is doing the only thing that matters. Past that, a jar and a screen on your own counter costs almost nothing. It puts the sourcing question entirely in your hands.
entries.short_answer: Yes, chosen well. Broccoli, radish or mung from the cold case, with white roots and no sour smell. Home-grown from organic seed works too. Skip alfalfa and soy sprouts. Weston A. Price guidance eats them lightly steamed, not raw.
entries.detail: Weston A. Price Foundation guidance accepts organic sprouting seeds with two exceptions, alfalfa and soybean. Alfalfa seeds contain canavanine, and raw sprouts hold irritants that are neutralized in cooking, so the guidance is to eat them lightly steamed or cooked. Sprouting has been a winter green in kitchens for a very long time, and a jar with a mesh lid on the counter still produces a crop in three or four days. Buying them is fine when the case is cold and turnover is quick; sprouts go slick and sour before they look wrong.
entries.kristy_take: A jar, a mesh lid and organic seed grow a crop at home. Bought sprouts come from the cold case; steam them lightly before eating.
buying_tips: Best: home-sprouted organic seed in a jar with a mesh lid, three days on the counter.

entries.title: Root vegetables: carrots, potatoes, beets
entries.question: How do I choose and store carrots, potatoes, sweet potatoes, and beets?
entries.decision: Local roots grown without sprays, fresh-dug, then organic.
entries.why: Roots grow in the soil and the skin often gets eaten, so how they were grown comes first.
entries.short_answer: Firm is the test at every root. Potatoes: no bruises, nicks or soft spots, never green. Carrots: well colored, no green shoulders, wilt, flab or cracks. Sweet potatoes: smooth, even shape, even peel color. Beets: round, slender tap root.
entries.detail: Top tier is local and in season from a grower who uses no sprays, then organic; ask the grower how the crop was grown. Potatoes keep up to a month in a cool, dark place with good ventilation, ideally 45 to 50°F. Throw away any that turn shriveled or green or grow many sprouts. Sweet potatoes want cool and dry, 55 to 59°F: colder brings chilling injury (fungal decay, internal browning, shriveling) and warmer speeds sprouting. Carrots go in a closed bag or container in the refrigerator for up to two weeks. Cut the tops off first, since attached tops wilt the root, and a wilted carrot revives in a soak of cold water. Beets: trim the leafy stem to an inch, leave the root end on, and refrigerate in a food-safe container for up to two weeks. Stored potatoes are often treated with a sprout inhibitor, so fresh-dug local potatoes come first.

entries.question: How do I pick fresh broccoli, cauliflower, or cabbage?
entries.decision: Local broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage grown without sprays, then organic.
entries.why: Tight, dark green broccoli florets are fresh. Enlarged, open or yellowish-green ones are past fresh.
entries.short_answer: Broccoli: dark green florets, closed, not yellowish or wilted, on stems that are not thick and tough. Cauliflower: no bruises or damage. Cabbage: strip wilted or insect-damaged outer leaves. A soft or slippery head stays on the shelf.
entries.detail: Top tier is local and in season from a grower who uses no sprays, then organic; ask the grower how the crop was grown. Broccoli is the short keeper of the three: refrigerate it in a plastic bag with holes and use it within three days. Cabbage goes the other way, staying fresh for several weeks in a plastic bag or wrap in the refrigerator at 41°F or below; before using, cut out the core and rinse the leaves under cool running water. Cauliflower gets kept away from raw meat and meat juices.

entries.title: Onions and garlic
entries.question: How do I pick onions and garlic that will keep?
entries.decision: Local onions and garlic grown without sprays, firm, dry-necked.
entries.why: A well-cured bulb feels dry at the neck and papery outside. A soft, scented or sprouting bulb is already on its way out.
entries.short_answer: Onions: firm for their size, little to no scent, a dry neck, no cuts, bruises or mold, no sprouting. Some loose skins are normal. Garlic: clean, white or true to the variety, well cured, cloves firm.
entries.detail: Top tier is local and in season from a grower who uses no sprays, then organic; ask the grower how the crop was grown. Whole dry onions live in a cool, dry, dark place with plenty of air movement: no plastic bags, no wrap, and not beside potatoes or anything else that releases moisture. Storage between 41 and 75°F favors sprouting, so the cooler the spot the better. Refrigeration is only for sweet or mild high-water varieties, on a low-humidity setting, and a cut onion goes in a sealed container for up to seven days. Garlic keeps one to two months at room temperature in low humidity before it softens, goes spongy, and shrivels from water loss; it sprouts fastest between 41 and 65°F, and its odor moves into other foods, so it gets stored on its own.

entries.title: Leafy greens: lettuce, spinach, kale
entries.question: How do I choose and keep lettuce, spinach, and kale?
entries.decision: Lettuce grown without sprays, local or living greenhouse, then organic.
entries.why: Spinach is highly perishable, and kale wilts in warmth. A leaf that still stands crisp tells you it has freshness left.
entries.short_answer: Lettuce: crisp, green outside, pale at the heart. Romaine: neither very loose nor very hard. Spinach: uniformly green and fully crisp. Kale: firm, deep colored leaves on moist, hardy stems.
entries.detail: Cold is the whole storage story. Romaine keeps about 21 days near 32°F and noticeably less at 41°F, so the coldest shelf of the refrigerator is the right one. Spinach wants 32°F too and will not hold good quality past two weeks; at 41 to 50°F it wilts and yellows faster. Kale goes in a plastic bag with as much air pressed out as possible, unwashed, for about five days; water on the leaves speeds spoilage, so wash at the point of use. Small greenhouse growers sell living lettuce with the root ball on, grown with no sprays of any kind; one says the root ball doubles the shelf life, and another packs it to stay fresh up to three weeks. Greenhouse or hydroponic alone does not say how it was grown, so look for the no-sprays word. In a big store, organic spring mix and romaine are the fallback. At the shelf, lettuce runs bright to dark green outside and yellow or light green at the heart, free of insects, decay, or damage. A very loose romaine head is immature; a very firm or hard one is overmature. Spinach should be fairly clean with no serious damage. Kale should show no browning, yellow, or small holes.

entries.title: Bell peppers
entries.question: How do I choose and keep bell peppers?
entries.decision: Local or greenhouse peppers labeled grown without sprays.
entries.why: A pepper should feel firm when you hold it. Wrinkled skin means it has lost water in storage.
entries.short_answer: Green peppers: judged on size, firmness, and color. Colored peppers: at least half colored, firm, and uniform in shape and size. Skip any with cracks, decay, sunburn, disease, insect damage, or bruises.
entries.detail: Peppers keep best around 45°F, three to five weeks, and shrivel from water loss when stored warmer. At 41°F they hold about two weeks before chilling injury begins to show as pitting, decay, softening, or a discolored seed cavity; red and other colored peppers are less sensitive to chilling than green ones. Keep peppers away from raw meat and meat juices. A dark, sunken spot at the blossom end is blossom end rot.

entries.title: Apples and pears
entries.question: How do I choose and keep apples and pears?
entries.decision: Local, in-season, uncoated apples and pears grown without sprays.
entries.why: Apples should feel crisp. A firm green Bartlett pear can ripen at home, turning sweet, juicy and buttery.
entries.short_answer: Apples: firm and crisp, not mealy, free of bruising, decay, cracks, and insect injury. Pears: sound shape and size, free of bruising, insect damage, and decay. A firm green Bartlett is not a fault.
entries.detail: Cold and dark is the storage rule: 30 to 32°F is best and up to 40°F still works, in a ventilated box or a plastic bag with holes, unwashed, since the moisture from washing hastens decay. Gala apples soften quickly, so cool them fast; McIntosh and Honeycrisp are prone to chilling injury and want 38°F. Refrigerated apples keep up to a month. Keep apples and pears away from raw meat and meat juices. Added edible coatings sit on the Weston A. Price Foundation avoid list, and orchards that skip synthetic sprays and wax coatings say so, so ask at the stand: waxed or coated? On apples, look for cracks at the stem or blossom end. Bartletts are picked mature-green and ripened off the tree; a ripe one is sweet, aromatic, and juicy with a buttery texture.
sources: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping Guide Categories

entries.title: Citrus: oranges, lemons, limes
entries.question: How do I choose and keep oranges, lemons, and limes?
entries.decision: Untreated, uncoated citrus from a grower, then organic.
entries.why: Yellow limes carry more juice. A partly green orange can be fully mature, so feel for a firm, smooth rind.
entries.short_answer: Oranges: even color, firm, smooth, free of decay and bruising. A partly green orange can be fully mature. Lemons: even yellow, smooth, firm, no shriveling. Limes: firm and smooth, no dryness.
entries.detail: Oranges keep at room temperature for up to a week and in the refrigerator for up to three weeks. Lemons hold best around 54 to 57°F and limes around 50 to 55°F, warmer than a refrigerator. A lemon or lime that has turned yellow is the one to use first: lemons picked fully yellow and limes picked yellow must be marketed quickly, while the fruit picked dark green keeps longest. At the bin, oranges should show even, intense color, free of skin blemishes and discoloration. A partly green orange gets its color from degreening, which does not change the inside. Lemons should be free of decay, drying, and rind stains. Green limes are preferred in the US, but yellow limes carry more juice; pick limes free of bruises and oil spotting. Conventional citrus is often treated after harvest with imazalil or thiabendazole fungicides, and residues are measurable in the peel, so organic or untreated is the pick, most of all when the zest goes in.

entries.title: Stone fruit: peaches, nectarines, plums, cherries
entries.question: How do I choose and keep peaches, nectarines, plums, and cherries?
entries.decision: In-season local peaches, plums and cherries labeled grown without sprays.
entries.why: A peach’s green background turns yellow as it readies. Unbruised fruit is the pick.
entries.short_answer: Peaches and nectarines: ground color turned from green to yellow. Plums: skin color turned for the variety. Cherries: at least light red all over, with green fleshy stems.
entries.detail: The optimum storage for all of them is just above freezing, 30.5 to 32°F, and Michigan Fresh puts cherries in the refrigerator at or below 41°F. Plums held between 36 and 46°F, the killing range, are more susceptible to internal breakdown: mealiness, browning, and failure to ripen. Peaches, nectarines, and plums picked well mature ripen on their own without ethylene; ethylene does not speed cherry ripening. Keep stone fruit away from raw meat and meat juices. On EWG’s Dirty Dozen, a standard ranking residues from USDA data, both peaches and cherries appear. A peach or nectarine with a flesh firmness of 2 to 3 pounds-force counts as ready to eat, and the same holds for plums. Dark skin staining is inking, a cosmetic mark from abrasion that affects the skin only. Cherries should be at least light red across the whole surface, with no cracks, bird pecks, shriveling, or decay; green, fleshy stems go with freshness.

entries.question: Which sandwich bread is whole wheat?
entries.decision: Sourdough or sprouted whole wheat bread, organic, short list.
entries.why: Whole wheat flour keeps the bran and germ along with the rest of the grain, in their natural proportions.
entries.short_answer: The top loaf is sourdough, soaked or sprouted, from organic whole grain flour, with no added gluten, soy or bran. A loaf called “wheat” needs an ingredient check; enriched grain and whole grain are different descriptions.
entries.detail: The top rung is sourdough, soaked or sprouted bread made from freshly ground organic whole grain flour, without additives such as added gluten, soy, bran or partially hydrogenated oils. Organic whole grain bread without those additives is the next rung. Most commercial bread is built on white flour with added gluten, soy and dough conditioners, and some adds ascorbic acid. The US whole wheat bread standard excludes ordinary flour, bromated flour and phosphated flour from the dough. A Basic Whole Grain Stamp may appear on a product containing more refined grain than whole grain. Potassium bromate and azodicarbonamide (ADA) are dough conditioners, so read the list for them.

entries.title: Sourdough bread
entries.question: How do you choose a traditionally fermented sourdough?
entries.decision: Whole wheat sourdough: flour, water, salt and a starter.
entries.why: A flour-and-water starter lets wild yeast and bacteria raise the dough and develop its sour flavor.
entries.short_answer: Traditional sourdough uses a flour-and-water starter containing wild yeasts and bacteria. Some bread labeled sourdough uses commercial yeast and added acids for sour flavor.
entries.detail: A true sourdough rises on its starter alone. If yeast is on the label, it is not a true sourdough, and the word “organic” or “sourdough” on the front still calls for reading the list. The long, warm, acidic fermentation of a starter reduces the phytic acid in the flour, and eight hours of sourdough fermentation has been measured to remove nearly all of it in whole wheat bread. The fermentation review describes acid formation and leavening by microbes. Culture or starter may not be listed separately, so the baker can clarify the process.

entries.decision: Soaked, cooked oats; if boxed, organic soaked granola.
entries.why: Cold cereal is made by extrusion, high heat and pressure. Soaked, cooked porridge is the traditional breakfast grain.
entries.short_answer: Boxed cold cereal is extruded: a grain slurry forced through a small hole at high heat and pressure. Organic boxes are made the same way. Soaked, cooked porridge is the top rung; organic soaked granola is the boxed fallback.
entries.detail: Modern cold breakfast cereals are made by extrusion. Grains are mixed with water into a slurry and forced out of a small hole under very high temperature and pressure; the shape of the die makes the flake, the O or the puff. The traditional breakfast grain is a porridge: whole grains soaked overnight and cooked, served with butter and cream. Unsoaked granola sits with extruded cereal on the low rung, and organic soaked granola is the boxed option. For oat cereal, certified organic skips glyphosate sprayed before harvest.
