entries.title: Mushrooms
entries.question: How do you pick good mushrooms?
entries.decision: Local mushrooms grown without sprays, then organic, dry and firm.
entries.why: Closed caps taste milder; open caps with gills showing taste stronger. Dry, firm caps are the fresh ones.
entries.short_answer: Choose mushrooms that feel dry and firm, with no dark spots. Closed caps taste milder. Open caps with gills showing taste stronger. Keep them cold in a paper bag.
entries.detail: A local grower who uses no sprays comes first, then organic. Look for caps closed around the stem or moderately open, with pink or light tan gills. The cap surface should be white, creamy or an even light brown. Portobello is a large, mature cremini. Shiitake has broad, umbrella-shaped caps and is best cooked. Store mushrooms unwashed in the refrigerator, in the original container or a paper bag. A plastic bag or airtight container collects moisture that spoils them. Use fresh mushrooms within a week for best quality. Only an expert can tell poisonous wild mushrooms from edible ones, and no amount of cooking or drying destroys the toxins.

entries.title: Green beans
entries.question: How do you pick good green beans?
entries.decision: Local, in-season beans labeled grown without sprays.
entries.why: A crisp pod with flat seeds is a young bean. Bulging seeds mean an older bean turning tough, stringy and starchy.
entries.short_answer: Choose green beans that are smooth, firm and crisp. Skip pods with bulging seeds, brown or rust spots, or a damp, sticky feel. Keep them cold and use them within five days.
entries.detail: Green beans are snap beans, eaten pod and all while the bean inside is still immature. Ohio State Extension describes good snap beans as firm, crisp and smooth, with no seeds bulging. Keep fresh beans cold and humid in the refrigerator and use them within five days if possible. Snap beans also come yellow, purple and red.

entries.title: Gluten-free bread
entries.question: How do you pick gluten-free bread?
entries.decision: Gluten-free sourdough or sprouted bread, short list, fewest gums.
entries.why: Blended flours and starches replace wheat. A gum binder gives back some of the stretch gluten would provide.
entries.short_answer: “Gluten-free”, “no gluten”, “free of gluten” and “without gluten” all meet one federal limit. The claim is voluntary. Bakers replace gluten with blended flours and starches, plus a gum that binds the loaf.
entries.detail: All four claim wordings mean the food has less than 20 ppm (parts per million) gluten under one federal labeling rule. Wheat starch may appear only if the food stays under 20 ppm. The claim is voluntary. Bakers replace gluten with a blend of flours and starches, such as rice, potato or tapioca. A gum binder, usually xanthan gum or HPMC, mimics some of the stretch gluten gives. Gluten-free does not mean unrefined. Many gluten-free breads and mixes are mostly starch, with added sugar and gums. Grains were traditionally prepared by soaking, sprouting or leavening with wild yeast, and gluten-free sourdough and sprouted loaves follow that.

entries.title: Pastries and bakery muffins
entries.question: Which fat is in a pastry or a bakery muffin?
entries.decision: Butter pastries and muffins, natural sweetener, whole grain flour.
entries.why: Butter is the traditional fat in pastries and muffins. Factory-made versions often swap in other fats.
entries.short_answer: Read the fat and the sweetener, or ask the baker. The top rung is butter or coconut oil, a natural sweetener and soaked or sprouted whole grain flour. Skip shortening, hydrogenated oil and refined sugar or corn syrup.
entries.detail: On the traditional tiers, the best muffins and baked goods use organic natural sweeteners, soaked or sprouted whole grain flour, and butter, coconut oil or another traditional fat. Most commercial ones use partially hydrogenated oils and refined sweeteners such as sugar, high fructose corn syrup or agave. Danish pastry is laminated, meaning butter is folded into a yeast dough in thin layers. Butter is the traditional fat; industrial production often uses other fats, such as hydrogenated sunflower oil. The American muffin is a quick bread, raised by baking soda instead of yeast.

entries.why: Cultured sour cream is soured by bacteria. Acidified sour cream is soured with added acids.
entries.short_answer: The tub names the method. Sour cream, or cultured sour cream, is cream soured by bacteria. Acidified sour cream is soured with added acids. Both hold at least 18 percent milkfat.
entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 131.160, sour cream is pasteurized cream soured by lactic acid bacteria. It may be named “Cultured sour cream”. Optional ingredients may improve texture, extend shelf life, or stop syneresis, which is liquid separating out. A flavoring that characterizes the product is declared with the name.

entries.title: Sauerkraut
entries.question: How do you pick sauerkraut?
entries.decision: Raw sauerkraut from the refrigerated case.
entries.why: Raw kraut goes from fermenting straight to the package. Shelf-stable kraut is heated in the jar or can.
entries.short_answer: Pick sauerkraut labeled raw from the refrigerated case. Raw kraut is not heated and keeps its crunch. Shelf-stable jars and cans are heated, which stops fermenting. Refrigerated alone does not prove raw.
entries.detail: Sauerkraut is shredded cabbage mixed with salt and left to ferment. Lactic acid bacteria, the microbes that sour it, turn the cabbage sugars into acids. Home recipes aim for 2.25% to 2.5% salt. Raw kraut is packaged straight from fermentation without heat, then kept refrigerated. Shelf-stable kraut is packed in a jar or can, then heated. The heat stops fermentation and gives a shelf life of a few years. Fresh-pack pickles get their acid from vinegar, while sauerkraut is a fermented pickle product.

entries.detail: Cider vinegar is made from apple juice by two fermentations. Yeast first turns the sugars into alcohol, making cider. The mother is a cellulose film of acetic bacteria. It may remain in unfiltered vinegar, or be filtered out.

entries.detail: Tempeh is cooked soybeans fermented with a Rhizopus culture, a mold, into a firm, dense cake. entries.title: Salt
entries.question: How do you pick salt?
entries.decision: Sea salt naming its sea, with salt alone listed.
entries.why: Sea salt carries its own water’s plastic, so a named sea and salt alone is the closest read.
entries.short_answer: Look for sea salt that names its sea or coast, with salt alone on the list. Sea salt tracks the pollution of its own waters, so a named source gives something to judge.
entries.detail: A systematic review of ten studies found microplastics in the majority of salt samples, from none detected up to 1,674 particles per kilogram in sea salt, 8 to 462 in lake salt and 0 to 204 in rock and well salt. A study of 39 brands across six continents found that unrefined sea salt tracks the plastic pollution of the seawater around it, unless the particles are filtered out during manufacture. That makes the sea of origin and the way the salt is processed the two things worth reading for. No tested salt type was clear across every sample, so a package promising zero microplastics needs a stated method behind it. Under 21 CFR 100.155, table salt with no added iodide must carry a statement that it “does not supply iodide” right after the name. An anticaking agent, an additive that keeps salt from caking, may be added under 21 CFR 172.490, and the list names it. Sea salt is made by evaporating seawater and usually has larger crystals than the fine grains of table salt. Flaked salt is a type of sea salt with larger, irregular flakes. Pickling or canning salt is pure salt with nothing added, and it keeps a brine clear. Kosher salt has a coarse texture, so salts do not swap cup for cup. Pink Himalayan salt is sodium chloride, like other salts. Curing salt, sometimes dyed pink and labeled “pink salt,” is a different product used for curing meats.

entries.title: Sugar
entries.question: How do you pick sugar?
entries.decision: Coconut or maple sugar first, each from one sap.
entries.why: Coconut sugar is palm flower sap and maple sugar is maple sap. White sugar is crystallized from cane or beet juice.
entries.short_answer: Coconut sugar and maple sugar each come from one sap. Cane sugar and beet sugar are the same sugar. Brown sugar is sugar with molasses added. Turbinado is a raw cane sugar, paler than brown sugar.
entries.detail: Sucrose is the name 21 CFR 184.1854 gives to sugar, cane sugar or beet sugar. It is crystallized from sugar cane or sugar beet juice, so cane and beet sugar are the same substance. Brown sugar is sugar with molasses added. Light brown carries approximately 3.5 percent molasses and dark brown approximately 6.5 percent. Raw sugar, also called turbinado, is a cane sugar with minimal refining, paler than brown sugar. Coconut sugar comes from the sap of coconut palm flowers and is made mostly of sucrose. A single-ingredient sugar must show a percent Daily Value for added sugars, without the words “Includes Xg Added Sugars.” A “†” symbol after that percent may lead to a footnote. Under Vermont’s maple rule, maple sugar takes all its sugar from pure maple sap, with nothing added.

entries.title: Maple syrup
entries.question: How do you pick maple syrup?
entries.decision: 100% pure maple syrup, darker grade, from a named sugarhouse.
entries.why: Most table syrups are mainly corn syrup. Darker maple carries the stronger flavor.
entries.short_answer: Look for “100% pure maple syrup” on the label. Table or pancake syrup is a different product, mostly corn syrup. Darker grades carry the stronger maple flavor; the taste for light syrup came from early candy makers.
entries.detail: Maple syrup is sap boiled down at a sugarhouse, about forty to one, until it reaches the legal density of roughly 67 percent sugar. Many syrups made to look like maple are fakes, and the main ingredient of most table syrups is high fructose corn syrup. Early American candy makers preferred lighter syrup because it crystallized better, and that demand is why light grades gained status. Darker syrup comes later in the season and carries the stronger flavor. Today all consumer maple syrup is Grade A, classed by color and taste: Golden, Amber, Dark and Very Dark. Maple syrup and maple sugar are both top-rung sweeteners on the traditional tiers.

entries.title: Vinegar
entries.question: How do you pick vinegar?
entries.decision: Organic raw vinegar or aged balsamic, 5 percent for pickling.
entries.why: Raw, naturally fermented vinegar is the traditional pick. Labels print acidity, and 5 percent is the pickling floor.
entries.short_answer: Read the percent acidity on the label. Canning and pickling recipes use 5 percent, and 4 percent bottles are sold too. Vinegar keeps almost indefinitely; best-by is about quality. On balsamic, only the full protected names carry aging rules.
entries.detail: Vinegar labels state percent acidity. Some state grain instead, a strength unit where 10 grain equals 1 percent acidity, so 50 grain is 5 percent. The acid in vinegar is acetic acid; as an ingredient, acetic acid is produced by fermentation or by synthesis. Once a bottle is open, harmless vinegar bacteria can cloud it, and a mother, a soft floating mass, can form when pasteurization was incomplete; both are harmless. Traditionally, wine vinegar was made the slow way: in the Orleans process, wood barrels of fermented alcohol liquid acetify for about 1 to 3 months. Most vinegar is now made from distilled grain alcohol, and the most common method today is the faster submerged method. As Il Post reports, the words aceto and balsamico on their own are generic; only the full protected names carry a rule. Traditional Balsamic Vinegar of Modena (DOP) is made from cooked grape must and aged in wooden barrels for at least 12 years, and at least 25 for Extravecchio. entries.detail: “Jam” and “Preserves” are standardized names. Jam is made from fruit and sugar at a fixed ratio: at least 47 parts fruit to 55 parts sugar for some fruits, and 45 to 55 for the rest. The finished jam is cooked to not less than 65 percent soluble solids. Jelly is made from the filtered or strained juice of the fruit. Pectin is the natural substance in fruit that makes it gel; commercial pectins are made from apples or citrus fruit. Special pectins exist for jars with less sugar or no added sugar. Those jars do not use sugar as a preservative, so some require refrigeration. When a jam names several fruits, they are listed in order of predominance. Sugar can weigh more than the fruit in a standard jam. By one extension definition, jam is a sweet spread that holds its shape, made from crushed or chopped fruit. Jelly is a firm gel made from juice. Preserves are small whole fruits or uniform pieces in a thick, gelled syrup. Home-kitchen (cottage-food) jam follows the same federal standard of identity for each product.

entries.title: Ketchup and mustard
entries.question: How do you pick ketchup and mustard?
entries.decision: Fermented or unsweetened organic ketchup; organic mustard of seed, vinegar.
entries.why: Ketchup’s federal standard starts from tomato. Prepared mustard is ground seed, vinegar, turmeric, salt and spices.
entries.short_answer: Ketchup is made from tomato with vinegar, sweeteners and spices. Fermented ketchup is cultured with whey and raw vinegar. Prepared mustard is ground mustard seed, vinegar, turmeric, salt and spices.
entries.detail: Ketchup’s federal standard, 21 CFR 155.194, accepts three names: catsup, ketchup or catchup. It starts from tomato concentrate or liquid from red tomatoes. Vinegars, sweeteners, and spices, flavoring, onions or garlic are its optional ingredients. Lemon juice or suitable organic acids may be added only to adjust the pH, a measure of acidity. The mustard description here is the USDA AMS commercial item description, a federal purchase spec rather than retail law. It calls for ground mustard seed, vinegar, turmeric, salt and spices. Yellow seed goes into its Type I and Type II mustards, and brown seed into Types III to IX. Yellow mustard is smooth, with a mild flavor and slight acid taste. Dijon is smooth and pungent, with mild white wine notes. Stone ground is coarse and pungent, with visible specks of mustard seed. Spicy brown is slightly thick. Gums and artificial colors are not permitted, and added water must be declared. As a food history site reports, the Oxford English Dictionary traces ketchup to ke-tsiap. In the Amoy dialect of Chinese, that word means a brine of pickled fish. Mushroom, walnut and fish ketchups stayed more popular in the States until the mid-1800s.

entries.title: Soy sauce and hot sauce
entries.question: How do you pick soy sauce and hot sauce?
entries.decision: Soy sauce, traditionally brewed, not made fast with acid.
entries.why: Traditional soy sauce ferments for months; a fast acid method takes hours. Wheat and gluten-free are label facts.
entries.short_answer: Traditionally brewed soy sauce ferments for months. A fast method makes it with acid in hours. Shoyu is about equal wheat and soybeans; tamari is mostly soybeans. Some fermented hot sauces have no added vinegar.
entries.detail: Classic soy sauce is made by microbial fermentation. Soybeans and wheat are inoculated with Aspergillus oryzae, a mold. Traditional soy sauce then ferments for months or even a year. A fast method makes hydrolyzed soy protein with acid in hours, called acid hydrolysis. A USDA AMS purchase description covers both methods; it is a federal buying spec, not retail label law. It names Type I, fermented, made from koji: wheat and soybeans cultured with Aspergillus oryzae. It names Type II, non-fermented, a blend made from hydrolyzed vegetable protein. Shoyu, the prevalent Japanese style, is made from roughly equal parts wheat and soybeans. Tamari is described as all or mostly soybeans, with no wheat. As TASTE reports, tamari began in Japan as a by-product of miso making. Liquid pooled at the bottom of the miso barrel, and it was used for seasoning. Wheat is a gluten-containing grain. A gluten-free claim means any unavoidable gluten is below 20 ppm, or 20 mg per kilogram of food. A hot sauce cooked with vinegar may fall under the rules for acidified foods. A fermented hot sauce with no added vinegar may follow a different review process. Traditionally, hot pepper sauce is made from a salted pepper mash aged in barrels, and one study aged it in oak.

entries.question: How do you pick canned soup?
entries.decision: Bone broth soup with a short list; homemade is better.
entries.why: Most canned soups lean on MSG and yeast extract for flavor. Bone broth makes the base, and homemade beats the can.

entries.detail: Under 21 CFR 101.61, sodium words on a label have set meanings per standard serving. Sodium free means less than 5 mg. Very low sodium means 35 mg or less. Low sodium means 140 mg or less. Reduced sodium, or less sodium, means at least 25 percent less than a reference food, and the label names that food and the percent difference. Salt is not the same word as sodium; salt means sodium chloride. No salt added means no salt went in during processing, and a soup that is not sodium free says “not a sodium free food”. On the shelf, a slightly dented can is fine, but skip deep dents the size of a finger and dents with sharp points on the seam. Dusty cans or torn labels may mean old stock. Dates on cans mark peak quality, not safety. In a cool, dry pantry, high-acid canned food keeps 12 to 18 months for best quality, and low-acid canned food, including vegetable soups other than tomato, keeps 2 to 5 years.

entries.title: Olives
entries.question: How do you pick olives?
entries.decision: Brine-cured olives, fermented in water and salt, nothing else.
entries.why: Fresh olives are bitter, and curing removes it. Brine curing ferments the fruit slowly, with water and salt.
entries.short_answer: Olives off the tree are very bitter, so they are cured before eating. Brine-cured olives ferment slowly in water and salt. Lye-cured olives are a milder style. Opened olives keep about 2 weeks.
entries.detail: Olives picked off the tree hold a very bitter compound called oleuropein. Curing leaches it out. The common curing methods are water, brine, lye and dry salt, and each gives a different texture and flavor. Water-cured olives stay slightly bitter, because water removes less oleuropein. Brine curing is a fermentation that turns the fruit’s sugars into lactic and acetic acids. It uses only water and salt, but takes a long time. Lye curing works quickly, and rinsing leaves a neutral olive that takes on flavors from vinegar and herbs. Salt gives olives their flavor and serves as a preservative. Salt curing has roots in ancient antiquity. Commercial table olives follow three main methods: Greek, Spanish and Californian. Greek-style olives are picked near full ripeness, at the purple stage, and cured in brine. Spanish-style green olives are treated with lye, rinsed, then fermented. California-style black ripe olives are lye-cured and darkened with air, then colored black with an iron salt. One review’s table puts debittering at 6–12 months for Greek, 1–7 months for Spanish and 1 week for California. The California method gives the mildest flavor and the least bitterness. USDA grade standards cover canned ripe olives (U.S. Grade A, B and C). USDA defines green olives as “completely fermented and cured” fruit of the olive tree.

entries.title: Seaweed
entries.question: How do you pick seaweed?
entries.decision: Organic sea vegetables named by kind; kelp sparingly.
entries.why: Kinds differ widely, and several products label the species inadequately, so read for the kind by name.
entries.short_answer: Look for the kind by name, such as nori, kombu or kelp, not just “seaweed”. Kinds differ widely. Brown seaweeds such as kelp are dried, then ground or chopped for food.
entries.detail: Brown algae are seaweeds of listed species, among them Laminaria, Macrocystis and Undaria species. They are harvested mainly in coastal waters of the northern Atlantic and Pacific. The material is dried and ground or chopped for use in food. Kelp is also used in spices and seasonings as a flavor enhancer. As a food additive, kelp is the dehydrated, ground product made from certain Macrocystis and Laminaria species. One study found the species labeling inadequate or inaccurate for several products. Iodine content varies widely by kind, from 16 µg (micrograms) per gram in nori to over 8165 µg per gram in one sample of processed kelp granules. In Maine, most wild sea vegetables are harvested by hand at low tide in early spring. Harvesters trim the blades and leave the holdfast, the base that anchors the plant, for regrowth. Seaweed harvesting is generally done in the spring and summer months. Bullwhip kelp does not keep well under refrigeration or by freezing, so its blades are dried for storage.

entries.title: Salsa
entries.question: How do you pick a salsa?
entries.decision: Fermented or fresh cold-case salsa, vegetables first.
entries.why: Fermented salsa is cultured with salt, not heated. A shelf jar is acidified and heat-processed.

entries.detail: Most salsa is a mix of low-acid foods, such as onions and peppers, with more acid foods, such as tomatoes. Vinegar or citrus juice, such as lemon or lime, often adds more acid. A shelf jar is an acidified food: acid is added to low-acid ingredients for a pH of 4.6 or below. pH is the measure of acidity. Federal rules also require an acidified food to be thermally processed, that is, heat-processed. Salsas are named among acidified foods. Foods stored, distributed and sold under refrigeration are outside that definition. For a shelf jar sold under inspection, a process authority reviews the recipe and sets its scheduled heat process. Some states have cottage-food laws that let home kitchens sell certain foods without inspection. In Virginia, for example, such a jar sells only directly to shoppers, such as at farmers markets. Its front label states it was processed and prepared without state inspection. Its label also names the maker, physical address and phone number. These are label facts about where a jar was made.

entries.question: How do you pick tortilla chips?
entries.decision: Organic masa chips in lard, coconut oil or olive oil.
entries.why: Corn cooked in limewater grinds into masa, a dough. Untreated cornmeal will not form one.
entries.short_answer: Corn for tortillas is cooked in an alkaline solution, usually limewater, then ground into masa. Some corn chips use corn that never went through that step. Masa and a trace of lime often show on the ingredients.
entries.detail: The step is nixtamalization: dry corn is soaked and cooked in a solution of slaked lime and water. Slaked lime is calcium hydroxide, called “cal.” The cooked corn, called nixtamal, is washed, then ground into a dough, masa. The word comes from Nahuatl, the Aztec language. Cornmeal from untreated corn cannot form a dough with water alone. Masa harina means “dough flour,” the powder ground from nixtamal. Masa flour made at scale is based on the traditional method. Restaurant-style chips are tortillas cut into wedges and fried. Most bagged chips are shaped straight from coarse masa dough and fried. For chips, Kristy’s standard is lard, tallow, coconut oil or olive oil. Skip seed oils; avocado oil fits only when the maker states it is pure and cold-pressed.

entries.question: How do you pick popcorn?
entries.decision: Organic kernels, home-popped in coconut oil, butter or lard.
entries.why: Plain kernels pop with no oil at all, so the cook decides on any butter, oil or salt.
entries.short_answer: Popcorn is its own variety of corn. Water inside the hard hull turns to steam, the hull bursts and the kernel turns inside out. Plain kernels pop in a paper bag in the microwave, no oil needed.
entries.detail: Popcorn is a variety of corn, Zea mays everta. Its hard outer hull is the pericarp. Inside, moisture runs about 13 to 14.5 percent of the kernel. In one study, 4 to 47 percent of kernels failed to pop, depending on variety. Two popped shapes are grown, butterfly and mushroom. Mushroom popcorn is often sold prepopped and coated with flavorings. For popping at home, Kristy’s standard is coconut oil, butter or tallow. Skip seed oils; avocado oil fits only when the maker states it is pure and cold-pressed.

They are deep-fried or blanched in fat or oil, then frozen. Blanching is a short cook in hot water or steam. The fries are finish-fried from frozen to develop color and crispness. Why it works: frying is first a dehydration process, meaning it drives water out of the food. The drier the food going in, the better the crust. So cooks fry once, freeze, and fry again. As food cools, moisture moves from the center to the surface. The second fry boils it off. The first fry also leaves simpler pathways inside, so water escapes more easily the second time. An air fryer is a convection appliance, meaning it circulates hot air. It cooks faster than an oven and gives a crisp outside. French fries cook well in one. For added fat, Kristy’s standard is tallow, olive oil, or coconut oil. Skip seed oils; avocado oil fits only when the maker states it is pure and cold-pressed. Look for thick-cut fries on the bag. Acrylamide forms during high-heat browning; it is a cooking byproduct, not an added ingredient.

entries.decision: Organic whole grain waffles, no dyes or enriched flour.
entries.why: The ingredient list shows whether the first ingredient is a whole grain. “Wheat flour” is not one.
entries.short_answer: Read the first ingredient. “Whole wheat flour” and graham flour are whole grain. “Wheat flour” is plain flour, not a whole grain flour. FDA has not defined grain claims on the front, so the list decides.
entries.detail: FDA draft advice counts a grain as whole when the kernel is intact, ground, cracked or flaked. Every part of the kernel stays in the same proportions as the intact kernel. Its ingredients are enriched flour, water, sugar, egg, oil, salt, flavorings, whey, leavening and emulsifiers or other stabilizers. Whole wheat flour is optional there. Its flours meet the federal standard for enriched flour or for whole wheat flour.

entries.decision: Pasture-raised white meat nuggets, one solid piece.
entries.why: “White meat” means 100 percent light meat, and “mostly white meat” means 66 percent or more.
entries.short_answer: The label words set the light meat. “White meat” means 100 percent light meat, and “mostly white meat” 66 percent or more. A plain “Chicken Nugget” is a solid piece of meat or poultry.
entries.detail: On poultry labels, “white meat” or “light meat” means 100 percent light meat. “Mostly white meat” means 66 percent or more light meat. “Natural proportions” means 50 to 65 percent light meat. A nugget is an irregular, usually bite-sized piece, usually breaded and fried, meant as finger food. “Chicken Nugget” with no qualifier means a solid piece of meat or poultry. “Chopped and Formed” beside the name means chopped and formed meat or poultry. With binders, extenders or water, “nugget” is only a fanciful name. A descriptive name then follows, such as “Breaded Nugget-Shaped Chicken Patties”. A product labeled “breaded” carries batter and breading of no more than 30 percent of the finished product. “Ice glazed” beside the name means an ice glaze set the breading. “Mechanically Separated Chicken” is poultry with most of the bone removed by machine, in a paste-like form. Its bone solids are at most 1 percent. For added fat, Kristy’s standard is tallow, olive oil, or coconut oil. Skip seed oils; avocado oil fits only when the maker states it is pure and cold-pressed.

entries.title: Frozen
entries.question: How do you shop the frozen aisle?
entries.decision: Plain organic frozen foods, frozen solid, picked up last.
entries.why: Food held at 0°F or below keeps its color, flavor and texture better than warmer food.
entries.short_answer: Buy only food frozen solid, and pick it up just before checkout. At home, keep the freezer at 0°F or below. For a closer look, ask about frozen pizza, meals or fries.
entries.detail: Food stored at 0°F or lower keeps its color, flavor and texture. Food held at 15°F may feel hard, but it is less solidly frozen than at 0°F. Over the same time, the 0°F food holds color, flavor and texture better. Freezing keeps quality but cannot improve flavor or texture. Processors flash-freeze food, which means freezing it very fast. Sellers keep it at 0°F or below to hold quality. Fast freezing makes tiny ice crystals. Slow freezing makes large ones that rupture cells, so moisture leaks out on thawing. Freezer burn shows as grayish-brown leathery spots where air reached the food. It can also show as white, dried-out patches that turn tough and dry. Folded foil can develop pinholes that let freezer burn in. Store shrink-film on meat breathes, so overwrap it to stop freezer burn. Freezer times and dates on frozen food mark quality only. “Do not refreeze” on a package is the packer’s quality advice. Quality can drop, and the packer cannot know home thawing conditions. Vermont’s rule has frozen display cases hold air at 0°F or lower. Each case there has a thermometer. A load line marks the top of the cold air at each end of the case. Cases sit away from door drafts, fans, lights and heaters. Thaw in the fridge, in cold water or in the microwave. Cooking from frozen takes about one and a half times as long.
